The systematic review presented in this report evaluates the potential benefits of accessible home environments for individuals with functional impairments. This review was conducted to support the development of WHO’s Housing and Health Guidelines. The primary goal is to provide the best available evidence from existing research to inform the deliberations of the Guideline Development Group (GDG). The review focuses on three key areas: (1) individuals with functional impairments who may benefit from home accessibility modifications, (2) various home accessibility features, and (3) the health and social effects of modifications aimed at improving home accessibility. The report is structured as follows: Background: Provides context on the relationship between home environments and disability, emphasizing the importance of accessible housing for independent living. Eligibility Criteria and PICO Framework: Details the Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcome (PICO) criteria used to guide the review, including inclusion and exclusion criteria. Search Strategies and Article Screening: Describes the process of identifying and selecting relevant studies. Data Extraction and Evidence Synthesis: Explains how data were extracted, quality assessed, and findings summarized. Findings and Discussions: Summarizes the results and discusses their implications. Comprehensive Appendices: Includes detailed information supporting the review. Background The United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (Article 9) guarantees the right of individuals with disabilities to live in accessible physical environments and have equal access to information and communication. An accessible home environment is critical for enabling independent living for people with disabilities. Homes lacking basic accessibility features can severely limit daily activities, confine individuals to restricted spaces, and violate their human rights, ultimately reducing their quality of life. Contrary to common assumptions, individuals with disabilities represent a significant portion of the global population. The World Report on Disability estimates that over one billion people, or 15% of the world’s population, have some form of disability. The relationship between aging and disability is also increasingly relevant, as longer life expectancies have led to a growing aging population, particularly in high-income countries. However, the fastest rates of population aging are occurring in lowand middle-income countries. By 2050, more than 20% of the global population is expected to be aged 60 years or older, with the European region projected to have the highest proportion at 37%. Aging-related functional impairments often result in poor access to home environments, jeopardizing safety and quality of life. Many older adults wish to remain in their homes and live independently, but inaccessible housing often forces them into institutional settings, such as nursing homes, which are associated with higher economic costs and reduced quality of life. Accessible home environments can prevent these outcomes and support independent living. Disability, as defined by the International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health (ICF), is an umbrella term encompassing impairments, activity limitations, and participation restrictions. It is not merely an attribute of an individual but an experience shaped by societal barriers, such as inaccessible environments. An accessible home can mitigate the disabling effects of impairments, allowing individuals to function independently within their living spaces. Accessibility and Home Modifications Accessible housing can be achieved through universal design principles or home modifications. Universal design refers to the construction and adaptation of housing that accommodates people of all ages, sizes, and abilities. Life Span Housing, also known as Lifetime Homes in the UK or Adapt Housing in Australia, refers to housing that adapts to an individual’s changing capabilities over their lifetime. For this review, an accessible home environment is defined as one that allows individuals with functional impairments to enter, exit, and move within the home independently. The relationship between the built environment and health has been extensively studied, but there has been limited focus on the accessibility of domestic home environments for individuals with functional impairments. Homes with barriers can increase the risk of falls and injuries, restrict social participation, and place additional burdens on caregivers and social services. Accessible homes, on the other hand, can improve quality of life and reduce dependency on external support. Systematic Review Objectives The systematic review aimed to evaluate whether individuals with functional or cognitive impairments living in accessible homes experience better health and social outcomes compared to those living in conventional or unmodified homes. The PICO framework used for this review included: Context: Domestic homes in community settings. Participants: Individuals with physical or cognitive functional impairments. Intervention: Living in accessible home environments. Comparison: Living in conventional or unmodified home environments. Outcomes: Health or social-related changes, such as injury rates, quality of life, mental health, dependency on social services, and social participation. Search Strategies and Study Selection Comprehensive search strategies were developed to identify relevant studies from multiple electronic databases, including MEDLINE, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, Embase, and PsycINFO. Searches were conducted without language restrictions, and studies published since 2004 were prioritized. A total of 26,782 records were initially identified, with 12,544 records screened after applying date restrictions and removing duplicates. Updated searches in 2018 identified an additional 6,162 records. Titles and abstracts were screened by multiple reviewers, and full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. Findings and Implications The review identified 14 studies that met the inclusion criteria. These studies provided evidence on the health and social benefits of accessible home environments for individuals with functional impairments. Accessible homes were associated with reduced injury rates, improved quality of life, enhanced mental health, and greater social participation. The findings highlight the importance of evaluating interventions aimed at improving home accessibility, particularly in the context of an aging population. This systematic review underscores the critical role of accessible housing in promoting health, independence, and well-being for individuals with functional impairments. It provides valuable evidence to inform the development of policies and guidelines that prioritize accessibility in housing design and modifications.
